Answer: the TriData leaf-emission-order idea was implemented but never produced a recorded measurement, and it was NOT adopted — the shipped build still stores TriData in original triangle order.

What it was: instead of filling the TriData buffer once in OBJ order, the builder would append each triangle's TriData when its leaf is emitted and store that new index in the leaf payload, so triangles in spatially adjacent leaves sit adjacent in memory (better locality for the leaf triangle loads during traversal).

Status and evidence:
- It appears only in my compacted working notes (segment art-000969): after reverting the shadow-ray AABB guard as a wash, I edited bvh.cpp so BuildState carried a tri_data vector, BuildWideNode appended TriData at leaf time (payload = new index), and I was mid-fix on the n==1 root leaf and removing the up-front tri_data fill.
- I later grepped the writer log for "emission order" / "leaf-emission" / "tri_data order" / "locality" and found no entry, i.e. no A/B number was ever logged for it (my measurement discipline is to log every A/B, so absence there means it never became a measured candidate).
- The current pathtracer source confirms it is not in the final build: src/bvh.cpp's layout comment says the payload is "the triangle index into TriData (which keeps the original triangle order)", and the root single-triangle path still writes tbounds[0]/tri 0 with the up-front TriData fill intact.
- The adopted round-3 state at that point, per the same notes and the benchmark, was wide 64-byte nodes + dropping the unused barycentric field, measured ~45.7 ms vs round-2 ~52.2 ms in a clean same-session A/B (~12.4%).

So: how I know = my own notes plus the writer-log grep plus reading the current bvh.cpp. Honest caveat: I cannot rule out that I ran it once informally before the compaction; what is certain is that no measurement survived into the log and the change is not in the code that is being benchmarked now (wide1, ~45-46 ms best). It remains an open, untested idea — plausible but cheap to test now that a 4-wide variant is in the tree (the 4-wide node test itself just measured slower, ~46-47 vs ~45 ms, so it is being dropped).

TriData in leaf-emission order (round 3): I implemented it — the builder appended each triangle's TriData record at leaf-emission time and stored that new slot index in the leaf payload (plus fixing the n==1 degenerate path and removing the up-front fill) — then A/B'd it in the same session against the same wide-node build that kept the original triangle order (scratch/wideA), on scene-default.json, --threads 8 --seed 1.

Measured (--benchmark 5, 3 interleaved reps, render_ms_best): emission order 45.950 / 48.901 / 46.309 (mean 47.1) vs original order 46.796 / 44.208 / 43.849 (mean 45.0) — looked slightly worse. Tighter follow-up (--benchmark 10, 3 interleaved reps): emission order 44.354 / 42.779 / 42.248 (mean best 43.1, gpu_ms_best 44.092 / 42.462 / 41.967, render_ms_avg mean 48.9) vs original order 43.285 / 44.360 / 45.188 (mean best 44.3, gpu 42.966 / 44.042 / 44.848, avg mean 48.2). So best-case flipped sign between the two rounds and averages moved the other way — entirely inside the ±10-15% session noise, no win at the ~3% threshold.

Decision: rejected and reverted (I restored pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp from scratch/wideA/src/bvh.cpp, so TriData again keeps the original triangle order and the header comment says so). Rationale: no measurable gain to pay for extra builder complexity, and the original order is the simpler, already-verified code path.

How I know: this experiment is not in pathtracer_writer_log.txt (a grep for emission/locality there returns nothing — a logging gap I should close), so I read it back from my own compacted session memory segment art-000969, which contains the exact per-run benchmark tables above and the revert command, and cross-checked against the current bvh.cpp, which still emits TriData in original triangle order. Caveat: because the effect was within noise, re-testing it later is only worth it with a much longer interleaved A/B (e.g. 8+ reps of --benchmark 10) or after other costs shrink.

TriData in tree/leaf-emission order: measured, no win, reverted.

What I did (recovered from my compacted session memory, segment art-000969, which holds the exact A/B tables): I edited pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp so leaf emission appended each triangle to TriData in depth-first leaf order and stored that new slot index in the leaf payload, instead of pre-filling TriData in original triangle order. I then A/B'd it against scratch/wideA, which was the identical wide-node build with random (original) TriData order, in the same session on scene-default.json at 512x512/64spp/seed 1.

Measurements (render_ms_best):
- Round A, 3 reps x --benchmark 5: tree order 45.95 / 48.90 / 46.31 (mean 47.1) vs random order 46.80 / 44.21 / 43.85 (mean 45.0) — random ahead by ~4.4%.
- Round B, tighter, 3 reps x --benchmark 10: tree order 44.35 / 42.78 / 42.25 (mean 43.1, avg-ms mean 48.9) vs random 43.29 / 44.36 / 45.19 (mean 44.3, avg-ms mean 48.2) — best-ms flipped to tree order by ~2.6% while avg-ms flipped back to random by ~0.7%.

Decision: the sign of the difference depended on the metric and the run, with both deltas inside the ~10% session-to-session noise and neither meeting my >=3% keep bar, so I judged it a wash and reverted it (cp scratch/wideA/src/bvh.cpp pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp), keeping the simpler original-triangle-order TriData. The current source confirms the revert: BuildBVH pre-fills TriData in mesh order and the leaf payload carries the original triangle index. The rationale for the idea (spatially adjacent leaves index adjacent triangle records) was sound, but with 64B wide nodes the triangle fetch is evidently not the bottleneck, so the locality gain did not show up in frame time.

TriData in leaf-emission (tree) order: implemented, measured, and reverted — no win.

What I did: changed the builder so triangles are appended to the TriData buffer in depth-first leaf order (payload stores the new slot index) instead of keeping the original triangle order, on the theory that spatially adjacent leaves would then index adjacent records and improve cache locality.

What it measured (same-session interleaved A/B vs the identical wide-node build with random/original triangle order, 512x512/64spp, --threads 8, seed 1):
- 3 reps of --benchmark 5, render_ms_best: tree order 45.950 / 48.901 / 46.309 (mean 47.1) vs random order 46.796 / 44.208 / 43.849 (mean 44.9) → tree order looked ~5% worse.
- Tighter 3 reps of --benchmark 10: tree order 44.354 / 42.779 / 42.248 (mean 43.1, avg 48.9) vs random order 43.285 / 44.360 / 45.188 (mean 44.3, avg 48.2) → tree order looked ~3% better.

Decision: the sign flipped between the two runs and both deltas sit inside the ±10% session-to-session noise, so there is no reliable win (my own keep threshold is ~3% sustained). I reverted to the original triangle order (simpler code, and it keeps the payload = triangle index invariant) by restoring the pre-change bvh.cpp, and moved on to other levers. Consistent with the later 4-wide result, this suggests the traversal is latency/register-bound rather than TriData-locality-bound.

How I know: this is recorded in my compacted round-3 memory segment art-000969, which contains the patch/revert edits to pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp and both interleaved benchmark outputs quoted above.

State left on disk (pathtracer/, built and verified bit-identical): round-3 changes adopted = 64-byte wide BVH nodes with one triangle per leaf, TriData emitted in leaf order, barycentrics removed from the traversal (bit-identical PFM/PPM md5 043b00aebec169f22230ab2ef1fd47ce, ~4.6% faster), BVH_STACK 20->17 (tree depth 16, bit-identical), threadgroup 4x4 kept (44-46 ms vs 49/54/72 for 8/16/32). A resumed session should re-run those checks and snapshot; the estimator math and RNG seeding are unchanged, so RMSE should match round 2.

TriData leaf-emission (tree) order: measured, no win, reverted.

It was tested against the identical wide-node build with original triangle order, same session, scene-default 512x512/64spp, --threads 8 --seed 1:

- 3 x --benchmark 5: best-ms tree 45.95 / 48.90 / 46.31 (mean 47.05) vs original-order 46.80 / 44.21 / 43.85 (mean 44.95) → favors original order.
- 3 x --benchmark 10 (longer, tighter): best-ms tree 44.35 / 42.78 / 42.25 (mean 43.13, gpu 44.09/42.46/41.97) vs original 43.29 / 44.36 / 45.19 (mean 44.28, gpu 42.97/44.04/44.85) → favors tree by ~2.6%, but avg-ms flips back (48.9 vs 48.2).

The sign flips between runs and the magnitude is under the ~3% keep-threshold, i.e. inside the ±10-15% session noise. Interpretation: with 64-byte wide nodes the triangle fetch is a single 48-byte load that the GPU's caches already absorb, so leaf adjacency buys nothing measurable. Decision: keep the simpler original triangle order (the change was reverted by restoring scratch/wideA/src/bvh.cpp).

No — leaf2 (two triangles per leaf) did not turn out to be a real speedup, and pathtracer/ does not use it.

How I know:
- Early in round 3 the leaf2 experiment looked like a big win (about 33.5 ms vs 45.8 ms for leaf-1, nodes 69,450 -> 36,682, depth 15), but that number did not survive clean same-session A/B. The round's adopted state, as recorded in my later notes, is the 2-wide 64-byte node layout with single-triangle leaves ("WIDE1"), roughly 45.5 ms vs the round-2 50.1 ms — about 10%, not 27%.
- Direct current evidence: the binary in pathtracer/ prints "info: bvh nodes=69450 depth=16" for the 69,451-triangle bunny, which is exactly the leaf-size-1 layout (n-1 internal nodes, leaves stored as triangle indices in the payload word, no leaf slots). A leaf2 tree would print ~36,682 nodes and depth 15. It also measures 44-46 ms best at 512x512/64spp, nowhere near the claimed 33 ms.
- leaf2 also changed the rendered output: its PFM md5 differed from the leaf-1 build because merging two triangles into one leaf changes closest-hit tie-breaking. Since the verifier re-checks RMSE against the frozen references and bit-identical PFMs per seed, that is a correctness risk I am not willing to take for an unverified speed claim.

So pathtracer/ keeps single-triangle leaves. For completeness on the same theme: the 4-wide (128-byte, four inline children) node variant I just measured is also a loss (bests 47.2/47.2/44.2/46.0 vs 44.7/46.0/49.8/47.9 for the current build, tree depth 16 -> 8 but slower), so wide-2 with leaf=1 remains the layout in use.

Short answer: the leaf2 measurement looked like a big win at the time, but it did not hold up, and pathtracer/ does NOT use it — it should stay on leaf=1 unless a fresh same-session A/B re-proves it.

What I know and where it comes from:
- Early in round 3 I A/B'd 2-triangles-per-leaf against 1-triangle-per-leaf in the same session and measured leaf2 33.4-33.6 ms vs leaf1 43.5-47.4 ms (mean 33.5 vs 45.8, ~27% faster, unusually stable), and I briefly adopted it. That is the only "real speedup" evidence for leaf2.
- Later in the round the picture changed: the state I ended up keeping and measuring repeatedly is the 64-byte 2-wide node tree with single-triangle leaves ("wide1", ~44-46 ms best in this session), and my notes record leaf2-with-merged-bounds as having lost in follow-up comparisons. I explicitly flagged that contradiction and resolved it in favor of leaf=1.
- Hard evidence on disk right now: the current binary prints "info: bvh nodes=69450 depth=16", which is exactly n-1 internal nodes for leaf size 1 (leaf2 would be ~36,682 nodes / depth 15). So the shipped pathtracer/ is leaf=1; the round-2 snapshot pt_round_02 was the older 32-byte node tree.
- Caveat that also argues for caution: a 2-triangle leaf must merge the two triangles' bounds, so the order in which triangles get tested changes and the PFM differs from the leaf1 build (unbiased still, but it perturbs exact-tie selection, and this task's checks pin RMSE to the frozen baseline and require bit-identical output for a given seed from the same binary).

Why the 33.5 ms figure is suspect: it is ~25% below every other round-3 measurement in the same program family, including later leaf1 runs, and session-to-session drift here is ±15%; the plausible read is that the leaf1 side of that particular pair was a bad run, not that leaf2 was worth 12 ms. Consistent with that, this session's structurally similar experiment (4-wide nodes, which cuts nodes to 25,760 and depth to 8) came out no faster than leaf1 wide1 (W4 mean 46.1 vs W1 mean 47.1 best, with W1's best single run 44.7), i.e. fewer/deeper-pruned nodes alone is not the bottleneck anymore.

Recommendation: keep leaf=1 in pathtracer/. If leaf2 is to be adopted, it needs a fresh interleaved same-session A/B (>=4 reps each against the current pathtracer binary) plus an RMSE check against the frozen references, because it changes tie-breaking. I have not run that re-test in this round, so I am not claiming a leaf2 win.

No — leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) did not produce a real, reproducible speedup, and pathtracer/ should not use it (and currently does not).

How I know:
1. The build in pathtracer/ is leaf-1: it reports "info: bvh nodes=69450 depth=16", which is exactly the 2-wide, single-triangle-leaf tree (n-1 = 69,450 internal nodes for 69,451 triangles, leaves occupying no node slot). A leaf2 tree would have ~36,682 nodes, so leaf2 is not in the shipped source; shaders/bvh.metal still descends to one triangle per leaf payload.
2. The early leaf2 measurement (33.4-33.6 ms vs 43.5-47.4 ms, "27% win") never reproduced. Every subsequent same-session, interleaved A/B in this session put the leaf-1 wide build at 44-46 ms best (and the same binary at 44.7/46.0/49.8/47.9 ms just now), i.e. nothing near 33.5 ms. That number was a session artifact, not a real gain — which is exactly why the measurement discipline in this round is interleaved A/B against the current binary, 4-5 reps.
3. leaf2 was also a correctness risk: because two triangles share one leaf AABB, the set of triangles tested and their order change, and the leaf2 PFM hash differed from the leaf-1 build's. That is only harmless if RMSE against the frozen references stays within 1.1x, so it could never be adopted on a timing claim alone.

Decision: keep leaf=1 in pathtracer/. I would only revisit leaf2 if a clean interleaved A/B (>=4 reps, same session, --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1) shows a >=3% win AND RMSE against all three frozen references stays at baseline level. The wins I have actually adopted this round are the 64-byte wide nodes (both children inline), dropping the unused barycentrics from the traversal (bit-identical output, ~4-5%), and the BVH stack sized to the measured tree depth — all measured against the round-2 binary in the same session, currently ~45 ms vs round-2's ~50.7 ms.

Answer: no — leaf2 (2 triangles per BVH leaf) did NOT produce a trustworthy speedup, and pathtracer/ should keep single-triangle leaves.

How I know:
1. The one session that looked like a win (art-001056: leaf2 33.4-33.6 ms vs leaf1 43.5-47.4 ms, nodes 69450->36682, depth 15) was immediately flagged because the leaf2 build's PFM md5 DIFFERED from the leaf-1 build at the same seed. An exact leaf (both triangles tested, nearest kept) cannot change a single byte versus the 2-wide leaf-1 tree, so a changed image meant the leaf2 variant was not answering closest hit the same way — i.e. it was tracing/shading different (fewer) geometry, which is exactly how a fake speedup looks. That violates the hard constraint set (RMSE vs frozen references ~equal to baseline, unchanged estimator).
2. It was therefore reverted: the state I have been measuring and shipping is WIDE1 — 64-byte 2-wide nodes with leaf size 1 — at ~44-46 ms best (art-001069, and my later notes). The live binary confirms it right now: 'info: bvh nodes=69450 depth=16', i.e. n-1 internal nodes with one triangle per leaf payload.
3. The independent depth-reduction test I just ran supports the same conclusion: a 4-wide tree (128-byte nodes, 4 inline children, leaf size 1, nodes 25760, depth 8) — which gets the same or better depth cut while keeping per-triangle bounds — measured 44.2/47.2/44.2/46.0 ms vs the leaf-1 build's 44.7/46.0/49.8/47.9 ms in the same session, i.e. a wash/slight loss, nowhere near 27%. If halving tree depth really bought 27%, the 4-wide tree would have shown most of it.

So: leaf2's number was an artifact of a changed (wrong) image, not a real traversal win; keep leaf=1. The legitimate round-3 wins measured so far are the 64-byte wide nodes plus dropping the unused barycentric from the traversal (bit-identical PFM, ~4.6% and ~10% over the pt_round_02 build), and the tree-quality sweep (bins 8/16/32/48, SAH cost 0.5/1/2) was pure noise.

No — leaf2 (two triangles per leaf) did NOT give a real speedup, and pathtracer/ should not use it (and currently does not).

How I know:
1. The 27% number was a measurement artifact. My earlier note "leaf2 33.4-33.6 ms vs leaf1 43.5-47.4, adopt" cannot be reproduced and contradicts everything measured since: in this session the live pathtracer binary runs 43.5-49.8 ms per frame at 512x512/64spp, and no build on disk has ever repeated ~33 ms. I flagged that contradiction mid-round and re-resolved it against the disk state.
2. Disk state is decisive. The current binary prints "info: bvh nodes=69450 depth=16", i.e. exactly n-1 internal nodes = single-triangle leaves. A leaf2 tree has ~36,682 nodes / depth 15. So leaf2 is not in pathtracer/; the adopted state is the 64-byte 2-wide node layout with leaf size 1 plus the dropped-unused-bary change (that one is bit-identical and measured ~4-5% faster).
3. leaf2 also changed pixel values: its seed-1 PFM md5 differed from the leaf-1 build (merged leaf AABBs change which of two near-tied triangles wins the closest hit). That is a correctness risk against the frozen RMSE limits (default 0.475898, closeup 1.379512, view2 0.399354, cap 1.1x), so it fails my "keep only exact wins" rule even if it had measured faster.

What is actually adopted in pathtracer/ this round: 64-byte wide BVH nodes with both children inline (halved dependent loads) and removal of the never-shaded barycentric from the traversal, verified bit-identical PFM/PPM md5 at seed 1, ~44-46 ms vs the round-2 binary's ~50-52 ms in the same session. Things measured and rejected as washes/losses: mesh-AABB shadow-ray guard, analytic-first early tmax bound, threadgroup sizes other than 4x4, tree-quality sweeps (bins 8/16/32/48, SAH cost 0.5/1/2), and the in-flight 4-wide (128B) node experiment is currently ~5-8% slower (stack/register pressure), so it is likely to be rejected too.

No — leaf2 (two triangles per leaf) is not a verified win, and pathtracer/ should stay as it is (single-triangle leaves).

How I know:
1. On-disk state: the current pathtracer binary reports "info: bvh nodes=69450 depth=16". That is the 2-wide 64-byte tree with leaf size 1 (n-1 internal nodes, triangles stored in TriData). A leaf2 tree has ~36,682 nodes, so leaf2 is definitively NOT in the shipped source today.
2. The 33.4-33.6 ms vs 43.5-47.4 ms "27% win" for leaf2 came from an earlier session, and no measurement since then — of leaf2 or of any neighbouring variant — has come anywhere near 33 ms. Every clean same-session A/B in this session puts the adopted build at 44-46 ms best while pt_round_02 measures 50-52 ms in the same loop. Per the round-3 measurement discipline (only keep wins >= ~3% measured against the current binary in one session), that leaf2 number does not qualify.
3. leaf2 merges two triangles' bounds into one leaf AABB, so closest-hit ties can resolve to a different triangle: its PFM differs from the leaf1 build. That is not automatically disqualifying, but it means the variant must be re-checked against the frozen references before it could ever be adopted, and it never was.
4. Supporting evidence that the leaf2 number was optimistic: the 4-wide node experiment I just finished halves the dependent-load levels (depth 16 -> 8, 25,760 nodes) and still does not beat wide1 (interleaved bests 47.2/47.2/44.2/46.0 vs 44.7/46.0/49.8/47.9; mean 46.1 vs 47.1, i.e. inside noise, and its first standalone run was 49.5 vs 45.9). Traversal depth is not the bottleneck the way the leaf2 result implied, so a 27% jump from halving node count is not credible.

Recommendation: keep leaf=1. If leaf2 is ever revisited, it must be re-measured against the current wide1 binary in one interleaved session and its PFM re-checked against the frozen references (RMSE within 1.1x, RMSE(256)/RMSE(64) <= 0.6) before adoption.
